articles.excerpt: What I Built I built Jarvis Control Center, a local-first browser agent that lets users control their computer with natural language. You can ask it to open websites, search the web, play YouTube vide…
articles.body: What I Built I built Jarvis Control Center, a local-first browser agent that lets users control their computer with natural language. You can ask it to open websites, search the web, play YouTube videos, manage tasks, and use connected tools. For example: “Open YouTube and play 11K by Seedhemaut.” Jarvis uses Gemma locally to understand the request, decide whether a tool is needed, and execute the browser action through Playwright. It saves users from repeatedly opening tabs, searching manually, and performing routine browser workflows. Demo The launch demo is available in the repository README: View the Jarvis Control Center repository The demo shows Jarvis receiving a YouTube request, opening the browser, searching for “11K — Seedhemaut,” and playing the result.

articles.title: 🦥 My Screenshots Folder Was a To-Do List That Never Reminded Me. So I Hired a Sloth.
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Open your Desktop. Go on, I'll wait. Chances are it's a graveyard of files called Screenshot 2026-10-21 at 0…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Open your Desktop. Go on, I'll wait. Chances are it's a graveyard of files called Screenshot 2026-10-21 at 01.58.44.png . Hundreds of them. Most have never been opened twice. Look closer and a pattern appears. We almost never take a screenshot to keep something. We take it to do something later: a friend's message asking for the slides "by Friday 5pm" a flight confirmation you need to check in for the address of the coffee shop where the meetup is a CORS error you'll "google tomorrow" A screenshot is an intention with no reminder attached. The Desktop isn't a mess. It's a to-do list that has never once reminded anyone of anything.

articles.title: Stop Snapshot-Testing Voice Conversations: Verify the Turn Protocol Instead
articles.excerpt: A real-time voice companion can behave correctly while its test suite reports failure. The usual culprit is not that “the LLM knows better.” It is that the test encoded an assumption the product never…
articles.body: A real-time voice companion can behave correctly while its test suite reports failure. The usual culprit is not that “the LLM knows better.” It is that the test encoded an assumption the product never promised: an exact sentence, a fixed callback order, or playback beginning within an arbitrary sleep interval. That creates an uncomfortable engineering tension. You do not want to dismiss failures as harmless AI variability, but you also do not want brittle tests blocking valid behavior. A better approach is to test the conversation protocol deterministically and evaluate the conversation content separately. For a Tencent RTC conversational AI application, that means verifying facts such as: User speech invalidates the previous turn. An interrupted response cannot resume later.

articles.title: AI is changing the developer career ladder 🚀
articles.excerpt: GitHub's latest developer career advice is refreshingly practical: AI can write more of the first draft, but it cannot own the engineering outcome for you. The skills to double down on: • Systems thin…
articles.body: GitHub's latest developer career advice is refreshingly practical: AI can write more of the first draft, but it cannot own the engineering outcome for you. The skills to double down on: • Systems thinking : understand the service, data flow, failure modes, and tradeoffs around the code. • Judgment : spot the plausible-looking AI patch that breaks security, cost, or production behavior. • Communication : turn a vague product request into constraints an agent, teammate, and reviewer can act on. Using Copilot or an agent is becoming normal. Being the person who can frame the task, verify the output, and ship it safely is still the hard part.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 233 — The Artemis Generation
articles.excerpt: On Episode 233 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rick Jenet are joined by Dr. Amanda Smith-Hackler, with the Universities Space Research Association, about entering the space workforce.
articles.body: On Episode 233 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and guest host Rick Jenet are joined by Dr. Amanda Smith-Hackler, the Director of Education for the Universities Space Research Association and Principal Investigator for the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) Scholars and STEM Workforce Development Programs, about the new and exciting opportunities available to young people seeking to enter the space workforce. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
